questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish a domain model from a data model?
options: They are the same thing, just different names for the same artifact
A data model always comes before the domain model in a well-run project

A domain model is a conceptual description of real-world business entities and relationships independent of any platform; a data model is the technical implementation of that domain inside a specific platform like Salesforce
Domain models only apply to Salesforce projects, never to other platforms
questions.explain: The domain model describes the business reality (Customer, Equipment, Claim) independent of software; the data model is how that gets implemented as Salesforce objects, fields, and relationships -- and the domain model should come first.

questions.q: In the warranty-claims domain model example, what is the cardinality between Equipment and Warranty Claim?
options: One Equipment can have multiple Warranty Claims filed against it over its life -- one-to-many
Many-to-many -- many pieces of Equipment can share the same Claim
One-to-one -- each piece of Equipment can only ever have exactly one Claim
There is no relationship between Equipment and Warranty Claim in this model
questions.explain: The domain model states a piece of Equipment can have multiple Warranty Claims filed against it over its life, which is a one-to-many relationship from Equipment to Claim.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a Claim's lifecycle (Submitted, Under Review, Approved/Denied, Closed) matters beyond just describing status?
options: Lifecycle states are purely cosmetic labels with no downstream effect
Lifecycle states must always map one-to-one to Salesforce picklist values with no exceptions
Lifecycle only matters for Service Cloud implementations, never other clouds
The lifecycle often becomes the backbone of the automation design later, since 'what happens on a state transition' is exactly the kind of question automation tools answer
questions.explain: The lesson connects lifecycle directly to later automation design (Chapter 3) -- the triggers for what happens at each state transition are exactly what Flow and Apex are built to handle.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does domain modeling often get skipped under deadline pressure, and what's the risk of skipping it?
options: It gets skipped because it's technically impossible to do quickly, and skipping it has no real risk

It gets skipped because it produces no visible object or field yet, but a domain model that's wrong in a fundamental way tends to surface its damage expensively after real data already exists in the wrong structure
Domain modeling should always be skipped, since it never affects the eventual data model
It gets skipped only on projects that don't involve custom objects
questions.explain: Domain modeling doesn't look like visible progress, so it's tempting to skip under pressure -- but a mistake caught on a whiteboard costs an hour, while the same mistake caught after launch with real data can mean a costly migration.

questions.q: Which three elements does this lesson say recur in every domain model worth drawing?
options: Custom objects, validation rules, and page layouts
Apex classes, triggers, and test methods
Entities, relationships (with cardinality), and lifecycle
Profiles, permission sets, and sharing rules
questions.explain: The lesson identifies entities (the nameable business things), relationships with their cardinality, and lifecycle (states and transitions) as the three recurring elements of a domain model.
